question: In normal operation, which computer commands the ailerons?
explanation: ELAC 1 normally drives the ailerons; ELAC 2 drives the elevators and stabiliser.

question: In normal operation, which computer commands the elevators and the horizontal stabiliser?
explanation: ELAC 2 has pitch; ELAC 1 has the ailerons. Each can take over from the other.

question: Which computers provide the aileron droop function?
explanation: Aileron droop, normal and alternate pitch and roll, direct law and autopilot order acquisition are ELAC functions.

question: How many SECs (spoiler elevator computers) are there?
explanation: SEC 1, 2 and 3 command the spoilers.

question: Which SECs can provide alternate and direct pitch control?
explanation: SEC 3 controls spoilers only; SEC 1 and 2 also back up the elevators and stabiliser.

question: Which computers control the speed brakes and ground spoilers?
explanation: The SECs control the spoilers for roll, speed brake and ground spoiler functions.

question: Which of these is a FAC function?
explanation: FACs handle rudder trim, rudder travel limit, yaw damping, alternate yaw, flight envelope and speed computations, and wind shear detection.

question: How is a flight control computer reset from the overhead panel?

options.text: By pulling its circuit breaker only
By selecting its pushbutton OFF then ON
It cannot be reset in flight

explanation: Cycling the pushbutton OFF then ON resets the computer.

question: How long is a flight control computer's power-up test, during which its FAULT light is on?
explanation: The test runs at power application or after a transient; FAULT goes out when it completes satisfactorily.

question: Does the A320 remain in normal law after a single failure of a sensor, electrical system, hydraulic system or flight control computer?

options.text: No, any failure gives alternate law
Yes, normal law is kept after a single failure
No, it goes to direct law
Only if the autopilot is engaged

explanation: The redundancy is designed so that a single failure does not degrade the law.

question: Which failure mainly leads to direct law?

options.text: Failure of the Blue hydraulic system

explanation: Losing all three inertial references leaves no attitude data for the protected laws.

question: What controls remain in mechanical back-up after loss of all electrical power to the flight controls?

options.text: The pitch trim wheel and the rudder pedals
The speed brake lever and the trim wheel

explanation: The stabiliser and the rudder are mechanically controlled as a last resort.

question: At the latest, when does High Speed Protection become active?
explanation: It can activate from VMO/MMO depending on conditions, and at the latest at VMO + 6 kt / MMO + 0.015.

question: At what speed does the autopilot disconnect automatically in high speed protection?
explanation: The AP disconnects at VMO + 15 kt / MMO + 0.04.

question: With full nose-down stick held in high speed protection, to about what speed is the aircraft limited?
explanation: Pilot nose-down authority is reduced so the speed is held near VMO + 16 kt.

question: In high speed protection, what happens to the bank angle when the sidestick is released?
explanation: Outside HSP a released stick holds up to 33°; in HSP the aircraft rolls level.

question: To what is the bank angle limit reduced in high speed protection?
explanation: The normal 67° limit drops to 40° in high speed protection.

question: What happens to the pitch trim in high speed protection?

options.text: It is handed to the pilot

explanation: Auto trim stops so the nose-up correction is not trimmed out.

question: Which of these is part of the recommended recovery from high speed protection?
explanation: Extend speed brakes, increase pitch and reduce thrust (or use A/THR).

question: Above 100 ft RA, when does the high angle of attack protection engage?

options.text: When the angle of attack exceeds α prot
When the speed falls below VLS

explanation: Below 100 ft RA on landing it engages when α max is reached.

question: Once α exceeds α prot, how does the angle of attack relate to the sidestick?

options.text: The stick commands a load factor as usual
The angle of attack becomes proportional to stick deflection, and auto trim stops
The stick commands a roll rate

explanation: Neutral stick holds α prot; full aft stick gives α max.

question: Can a pilot stall an A320 in normal law by pulling the sidestick fully back?

options.text: No, α max cannot be exceeded

explanation: Full aft stick holds α max, a small margin from the stall angle of attack.

question: To what is the bank angle limit reduced when high angle of attack protection is active?
explanation: The 67° limit is reduced to 45° in high angle of attack protection.

question: What is VLS?

options.text: The lowest selectable speed, giving an appropriate margin to the stall
The landing reference speed in CONF FULL

explanation: The autopilot will not go below VLS with autothrust active.

question: What is green dot speed?

options.text: The maximum speed with slats extended
The best lift-to-drag ratio speed in the clean configuration

explanation: Green dot is used as the engine-out and holding reference in the clean configuration.

question: What is α floor in CONF 0?
explanation: α floor is 9.5° clean, 15° in CONF 1 and 2, 14° in CONF 3 and 13° in CONF FULL.

question: What is α floor in CONF FULL?
explanation: It falls as flaps extend: 15° in CONF 1/2, 14° in CONF 3, 13° in CONF FULL.

question: When can alpha floor engage?

options.text: From lift-off until 100 ft RA before landing
At any time on the ground

explanation: It is armed through the flight, but not in the last 100 ft before touchdown.

question: Besides α floor itself, what other trigger can activate alpha floor?

options.text: Sidestick deflection above 14° with high angle of attack or pitch attitude protection active

explanation: A large aft stick input in a protection is treated as a sign the pilot needs thrust.

question: When is alpha floor inhibited?

options.text: Above Mach 0.6, or with the TCAS mode engaged

explanation: TCAS manoeuvres and high Mach are excluded.

question: What does alpha floor do to the thrust?

options.text: Sets TOGA thrust regardless of thrust lever position

explanation: Thrust lever positions are ignored when alpha floor is active.

question: How is alpha floor shown on the FMA?

options.text: A.FLOOR with a flashing amber box

explanation: It appears in the first (autothrust) column.

question: After alpha floor, what does the FMA show when TOGA thrust remains locked?
explanation: TOGA LK stays until the crew disconnects autothrust, sets the levers and re-engages A/THR.

question: What is the load factor limit in normal law in the clean configuration?
explanation: Load factor protection lets the pilot pull full aft without overstressing the aircraft.

question: What is the load factor limit in normal law with slats or flaps extended?
explanation: The limit is lower with high lift devices extended.

question: When does the G LOAD indication appear in amber on the lower ECAM?

options.text: Above 1.4 g or below 0.7 g for more than 2 seconds

explanation: It appears on the system display as a crew awareness cue.

question: In CONF 0 to 3, what is the nose-up pitch attitude limit?

options.text: 30°, reduced progressively to 25° at low speed

explanation: In CONF FULL the limit is 25°, reduced to 20° at low speed.

question: What is the nose-down pitch attitude limit?
explanation: Pitch is limited to 15° nose down.

question: At what pitch attitudes do the flight director bars disappear?
explanation: They return at 22° up or 10° down.

question: What is the maximum bank angle with the sidestick held fully laterally in normal law?
explanation: 67° corresponds to the 2.5 g limit in a level turn.

question: In normal law the sidestick is released at 50° of bank. What happens?

options.text: The bank reduces automatically to 33° and is held there

explanation: Up to 33° the bank is held with a neutral stick; above it, the aircraft rolls back to 33°.

question: Above what bank angle does the autopilot disconnect and the FD bars disappear?
explanation: They return below 40°.

question: After take-off, up to what radio height is the reactive windshear warning available?
explanation: It starts a few seconds after lift-off. On landing it is available from 1 300 ft RA down to 50 ft RA, with at least CONF 1.

question: How is a predictive or reactive windshear warning presented?

options.text: A red WINDSHEAR message on both PFDs and the voice 'WINDSHEAR' three times
An amber caution with a single chime
A flashing A/THR on the FMA
A green memo on the ECAM

explanation: The crew sets TOGA and follows the SRS pitch order on the FD.

question: What is the low energy aural alert?
explanation: It asks the crew to increase thrust to recover a positive flight path.

question: In which configurations is the low energy warning available?
explanation: It is computed by the FAC from configuration, deceleration and flight path angle.

question: In which height band is the low energy warning available (outside it, it is inhibited)?
explanation: It is inhibited below 100 ft RA and above 2 000 ft RA, among other conditions.

question: Which failure leads to alternate law with reduced protection?
explanation: Double ADR or IR failures, both ELACs, one elevator, one sidestick, all spoilers, all SECs or a THS jam all give alternate law.

question: Loss of the Green and Yellow hydraulic systems gives which law?

options.text: Alternate law with reduced protection and mechanical yaw control

explanation: Without Green and Yellow, yaw falls back to the mechanical path.

question: Failure of all three ADRs gives which law?
explanation: Without air data, the speed-based protections cannot work.

question: In alternate law with the autopilot off, what happens to the law when the landing gear is extended?

options.text: It changes to abnormal attitude law

explanation: There is no flare mode in alternate law, so direct law gives the pilot a natural feel for landing.

question: In alternate law with reduced protection, which protection remains?
explanation: Load factor protection stays; α and overspeed protections are lost, replaced by speed stability.

question: In alternate law, what does speed stability do?

options.text: It pushes the nose down near the stall warning speed and pulls it up at high speed, but can be overridden
It locks the speed at the selected value
It acts only on the thrust

explanation: It is not a protection: sidestick inputs overrule it.

question: In alternate law, how is roll controlled?

options.text: As in normal law, with a roll rate demand
In direct mode, without bank angle protection or turn coordination

explanation: Roll becomes direct; yaw damping is still available.

question: Above what bank angle does abnormal attitude law engage?
explanation: Abnormal attitude law also engages beyond 50° pitch up, 30° pitch down or extreme speeds and angles of attack.

question: At what pitch attitudes does abnormal attitude law engage?

options.text: Above 50° nose up or 30° nose down

explanation: These are far beyond the normal law limits of 30° up and 15° down.

question: After recovery from abnormal attitude law, what law remains?

options.text: Pitch and yaw stay in alternate law for the rest of the flight

explanation: Flight controls stay degraded after an abnormal attitude.

question: Which PFD message tells the crew that the aircraft is in direct law?

options.text: MAN PITCH TRIM ONLY in red
USE MAN PITCH TRIM in amber

explanation: Direct law has no auto trim, so the crew must trim manually.

question: In direct law, how is pitch controlled?

options.text: Sidestick inputs move the elevators directly, with no auto trim

explanation: Auto trim and speed stability are lost.

question: On the F/CTL page, when is a spoiler shown as a green triangle?

options.text: When it is deflected more than 2.5°

explanation: A green line shows a retracted spoiler.

question: What does an amber PITCH TRIM legend on the F/CTL page mean?

options.text: The trim is at its limit

explanation: A jammed THS is one of the causes of alternate law.

question: On the F/CTL page, what does an amber rudder travel limiter indication mean?

options.text: The rudder is at full deflection
Both rudder travel limiters have failed

explanation: The rudder travel limiter reduces rudder authority as speed increases.

question: On the F/CTL page, what does an amber ELAC or SEC number mean?

options.text: That computer has failed or is switched OFF

explanation: Green numbers show available computers.

question: How many FLAPS lever positions are there?
explanation: Intermediate lever positions cannot be selected.

question: What slat angle is set in CONF 1?
explanation: CONF 1 is 18° slats with 0° flaps in flight, or 10° flaps (1+F).

question: What slat and flap angles are set in CONF FULL?
explanation: FULL is the normal landing configuration.

question: What slat and flap angles are set in CONF 2?
explanation: CONF 2 and CONF 3 share 22° slats.

question: What is the maximum speed in CONF 1?
explanation: VFE is 230 kt in CONF 1, 215 kt in CONF 2, 185 kt in CONF 3, 177 kt in CONF FULL.

question: What is the maximum speed in CONF 2?
explanation: VFE CONF 2 is 215 kt.

question: What is the maximum speed in CONF 3?
explanation: VFE CONF 3 is 185 kt.

question: What is the maximum speed in CONF FULL?
explanation: VFE CONF FULL is 177 kt.

question: Why are there stops at FLAPS lever positions 1 and 3?

options.text: To lock the lever in flight
To prevent excessive flap or slat travel being selected in a single action
To prevent selecting FULL on the ground

explanation: The lever must also be pulled out of each detent before it can move.

question: After a CONF 1+F take-off, if CONF 0 is not selected, when do the flaps retract automatically?
explanation: The automatic retraction protects the flaps from overspeed.

question: After flap retraction, when does CONF 1+F become available again (without having selected 2, 3 or FULL)?

options.text: When the airspeed is 100 kt or less

explanation: From CONF 0 in flight, CONF 1 gives slats only.

question: Where is there a detent on the SPEED BRAKE lever?
explanation: The lever has to be pushed down to move to the selected position.

question: How are the ground spoilers armed?

options.text: By pulling the SPEED BRAKE lever up in the RET position
By pushing the lever down at FULL

explanation: Armed ground spoilers extend at landing or in a rejected take-off.

question: If the ground spoilers are not armed, what else makes them extend automatically at landing?
explanation: Reverse selection also triggers automatic ground spoiler extension.

question: What effect does the RUD TRIM rotary switch have with the autopilot engaged?
explanation: The rudder trim switch and the RESET pushbutton are inactive with the AP engaged.

question: At what rate does the rudder trim RESET pushbutton return the trim to zero?
explanation: The trim runs back at 1.5°/s.

question: What is the range of the rudder trim position indicator?
explanation: The indicator shows the direction (L or R) and value.

question: What priority does the mechanical pitch trim wheel have over electric trim?

options.text: The trim wheel has priority over electrical control
The wheel works only on the ground

explanation: The wheels give direct mechanical control of the THS.

question: What happens to the autopilot if a pilot moves the pitch trim wheel in flight?

options.text: It switches to its other channel

explanation: Manual trim inputs and autopilot cannot coexist.

question: Does using the pitch trim wheel disconnect the ELACs?

options.text: No, so the computers stay synchronised with the manually selected position

explanation: Keeping the ELACs engaged avoids a jump when automatic trim resumes.

question: With auto trim in normal law and a neutral sidestick, what does the system maintain in level flight?

options.text: 1 g, with no pilot correction needed for speed, turns or configuration

explanation: Auto trim works with the load factor demand law, even with the autopilot off.
